name: Jade Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jade, and thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything here is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We rent 40 hectares from the county council's smallholdings, so the council is our landlord. I've got pastured pigs, 300 laying hens, a hectare and a half of vegetables and some oats for the pigs. Most of what we grow goes into a veg box scheme: 140 local households pay each month and get a box every Thursday. Mornings are animals, middles are picking and packing, evenings are emails and planning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI come into that, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use a chatbot to plan what to sow so the boxes aren't all courgettes in August, and to draft the Thursday newsletter. It also sorts the box orders and swaps, which used to eat my Sunday nights. My partner Sam teases me that I talk to it more than to him, which is fair. Money's tight, we've got under a month saved and a mortgage, but the box list has grown from 90 to 140 in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a useful tool for small farms, hype or not, and I'd keep sharing tips in the small growers' group chat. I'd say the real fight is supermarket prices and access to land. On my farm page I'd probably post a joke about the robot uprising being cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little for me, because I already get most of what I need out of the tools. My worries are the same ones: the council rent, feed prices and whether customers keep paying when money's tight. If the economy slows down, the veg boxes are the first thing people cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the box list, aiming for 180 households by next autumn. I'd add a farm-gate egg stall with an honesty box to bring in a bit of extra cash. And I'd keep using the AI for the planning and newsletter, since that's already paying off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little restless. I like having the plan in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a lot of box customers cancel at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're in trouble within about six weeks, because the box money pays the feed bill. Last January eleven people paused their boxes after Christmas and I had to sell two weaners early. I learned to keep the pig feed account paid a month ahead when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sam think of how hard you're pushing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam works as a teaching assistant at Mei and Ollie's school, so he sees the bills and he sees me up at eleven doing order lists. He says go for it but please sleep. I usually don't.

say: AI is still a **useful tool** for small farms, hype or not.
The real fight is **supermarket prices** and access to land.
think: The plateau changes little because I **already use** the tools well.
In a slow economy, **veg boxes** are the first thing people cancel.
do: Grow the box scheme to **180 households** by next autumn.
Set up a **farm-gate egg stall** with an honesty box.
Keep using AI for **planting plans** and the newsletter.
feel: **Mostly fine**, a little restless, liking the plan in her own hands.
S0.quote: If the economy slows down, the veg boxes are the first thing people cancel.
fieldNote: She feels **in control**, but her income depends on households' spare money.
Last January's cancellations forced her to **sell weaners early**, a real scar.
She uses AI daily and talks about it as **ordinary kit**, not a big deal.

steps.text: Grow the veg box scheme from 140 to 180 households
Set up a farm-gate egg stall with an honesty box
Use the chatbot to plan sowings so boxes stay varied

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farmers who learn the tools will be fine, and the state should pay for training so nobody's left behind. I'd post guides in the growers' group. I'd also say the big supermarkets will use AI to squeeze suppliers even harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one's good for me. The thinking jobs on my farm are the boring ones: ordering, invoicing, answering customer emails. If the software does those, I get my evenings back. The robots coming slowly means my pigs and veg still need my hands for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI customer service bot for the box scheme, so swaps and pauses are handled without me. I'd get the three other small farms in the valley to form a machinery co-op, so we're ready to share robots later. I'd use the evenings I save to start a second box round in the next town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a pinch of guilt. Some people's office jobs are going and I'm getting my evenings back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you worry about in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam's sister Lucy, who does claims at an insurance firm. That's exactly the work the card describes. I'd want to help her, maybe even get her working on the box scheme's accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think the other farms would join a co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Frank at Hillside already borrows my trailer every week, so the sharing is half done. The Okafors are younger and keen. The fourth farm would take convincing, but they hate the dealer prices as much as anyone.

say: Small farmers who learn the tools will be fine, with **state-paid training**.
Supermarkets will use AI to **squeeze suppliers** even harder.
think: The thinking jobs on my farm are the **boring ones** I'd happily lose.
Slow robots mean my **pigs and veg** need my hands for years.
do: Set up an **AI customer bot** for box swaps and pauses.
Form a **machinery co-op** with three valley farms.
Start a **second box round** in the next town.
feel: **Excited**, with a pinch of **guilt** about others losing office work.
S1.quote: The thinking jobs on my farm are the boring ones: ordering, invoicing, answering customer emails.
fieldNote: For her, Steady Disruption **frees time** rather than taking work.
Her progressive views show in wanting **shared ownership** of machines.
She worries for **Sam's sister Lucy**, whose office job is directly exposed.

steps.text: Set up an AI bot to handle box swaps and pauses
Form a machinery-sharing co-op with three valley farms
Start a second veg box round in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that robots and AI must be owned in common, or rural places get hollowed out. I'd push the growers' group to lobby for public money for farm co-ops. Online I'd be the annoying one posting every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, 2028 doesn't scare me much, because the thinking side of my farm is small and I'd use AGI happily. It's 2031 that worries me. A big robot farm could make my veg box look like a luxury nobody can afford. And by then lots of my customers might have lost their jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the co-op legally set up and apply for every grant going, before the money runs out. I'd use AGI to run the whole business side so I can grow more for less. And I'd sign up the box scheme as a supplier to the school kitchens, because councils pay on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lot of energy behind it. I'd rather be running than standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the box scheme if half your customers lost their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd lose half the box money, roughly, and that's the pig feed and part of the mortgage. I'd try a pay-what-you-can box for people who've lost work. I couldn't stand dropping families who've been with us for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AGI happily. Do you see any contradiction with your worries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. I'd use the same thing that's emptying my customers' wallets. I'd rather the tool were public, like the library, but I'm not going to refuse it on principle while the bills pile up.

say: Robots and AI must be **owned in common**, or rural places get hollowed out.
Farm co-ops need **public money**, and I'll keep posting about it every day.
think: AGI in 2028 doesn't scare me; **2031 robot farms** do.
My customers could **lose jobs** and cancel boxes at the same time.
do: Register the **co-op legally** and apply for every grant.
Run the whole **business side** with AGI.
Supply the **school kitchens** because councils pay on time.
feel: **Anxious**, but full of **energy** and wanting to keep moving.
S2.quote: A big robot farm could make my veg box look like a luxury nobody can afford.
fieldNote: Her risk comes through **customers' incomes**, not her own tasks.
She names her own **contradiction**: using what she fears.
A **pay-what-you-can box** shows her values under pressure.

steps.text: Register the valley machinery co-op and apply for grants
Lobby the council for public money for farm co-ops
Hand all ordering, invoicing and emails to AGI
Bid to supply vegetables to the local school kitchens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get co-ops and public ownership ready if we start today. I'd organise a meeting in the village hall. I'd invite the council farm estate people too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2034 is good timing for me. By then the co-op could own a shared weeding robot and a feeding robot for the pigs. Small farms working together could compete with the big ones, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the co-op over the first two years and save into a shared machine fund. I'd take an online course in farm robotics, so I understand what we're buying. I'd use AGI for planning and selling right from 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not. Five years is a proper runway for a small farm, if we start today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mei and Ollie's lives look like by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei would be nineteen, so she'd be choosing work right as the robots come in. I'd want her to learn how this stuff works, not just use it. Ollie would be sixteen and probably still obsessed with the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the co-op plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People fall out, mostly. Frank and the Okafors have different ideas of what tidy means. If the co-op broke up, I'd be a tiny farm against robot giants on my own.

say: Five years is enough to get **co-ops** ready if we start today.
Come to the **village hall meeting** and bring the council farm estate people.
think: Robots around 2034 is **good timing** for a shared co-op machine.
Small farms together could **compete** with big ones, maybe.
do: Build the co-op over **two years** with a shared machine fund.
Take an **online robotics course** before buying.
Use **AGI for planning** and selling from 2031.
feel: **Uneasy** but **more hopeful** than not, with a proper runway.
S3.quote: Five years is a proper runway for a small farm, if we start today.
fieldNote: Time turns her worry into a **co-op plan** she believes in.
The weak point is **people falling out**, not money or technology.
She wants her daughter to **understand machines**, not just use them.

steps.text: Hold a village hall meeting to start the farm co-op
Complete an online farm robotics course in the first year
Buy a shared weeding robot through the co-op by 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd say farmers should be at the table when rules are written. I'd keep posting guides and co-op tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one barely worries me. Robots in 2039 come when I'm 56, and with ten years I can build the co-op, grow the box list and maybe buy a bit of land. My worries go back to the ordinary ones, like the council rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm growing steadily and use AI tools to save time. I'd start putting money into the kids' college funds, even small amounts. I'd join the regional land campaign for longer council tenancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only in the normal way, and quite hopeful. It's the most like my real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider leaving farming in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather change the farm than leave the farm. Maybe I'd spend part of the week teaching small farmers to use the tools. That could be paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money tightens in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, which we barely take anyway. Then the new polytunnel I've been dreaming about. Never the kids' clubs.

say: Ten years is **a gift** we'd be fools to waste.
Farmers should be **at the table** when the rules are written.
think: Robots in 2039 arrive when I'm 56, giving time to **build the co-op**.
My worries go back to ordinary ones like **council rent**.
do: Keep **growing the farm** steadily with AI tools.
Start small **college funds** for Mei and Ollie.
Join the **regional land campaign** for longer council tenancies.
feel: **Uneasy** only in the normal way, and **quite hopeful**.
S4.quote: I'd rather change the farm than leave the farm.
fieldNote: The long timeline puts her back among **ordinary farm worries**.
Teaching others to use AI could become **paid side work**.
Her cuts protect **the kids' clubs** above everything.

steps.text: Keep growing the box scheme with AI planning tools
Open small college savings accounts for Mei and Ollie
Join the regional campaign for longer council farm tenancies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because robot farms in 2031 could make my boxes look like a luxury just when my customers are losing work. What would help is public money for farm co-ops and longer council tenancies, so small farms can share robots instead of being crushed by them. Free training wouldn't hurt either.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll still want a carrot with soil on it. I think lots of people will, more than ever, when everything else is made by machines. A robot can grow a carrot, but it can't tell a family which field it came from.

headlineQuote: A robot can grow a carrot, but it can't tell a family which field it came from.
portrait: Jade, 43, rents a **40-hectare** council smallholding with pigs, hens and a veg box scheme.
She uses AI **every day** for planning, orders and her newsletter, and her partner Sam is a teaching assistant.
Money is thin, but she feels **in control** because her customer list keeps growing.
Her answer to robots is a **machinery co-op** shared with neighbouring small farms.
She worries less about her tasks and more about **customers' incomes** if robot farms arrive fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because cheap robot farms could arrive just as her customers lose work.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for farm co-ops and longer council tenancies, plus free training.
